newsitem.title: USA: Dole urges on voters after break in marathon.
newsitem.headline: Dole urges on voters after break in marathon.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole resumed his campaign marathon on Sunday after a six-hour break. He took a turn at a party phone bank and told Republican volunteers his momentum was surging.
"We are excited about the direction of this campaign. All across America polls are going our way," Dole said after a brief stint working the phones at a local party headquarters.
"I just talked to four people, and seven of 'em had already voted," he joked.

The final weekend of the campaign was billed as a "non- stop" 96-hour marathon across the country. But Dole managed to work in a six-hour break on Sunday in the California beach community of La Jolla to nap and clean up.

Dole's press secretary Nelson Warfield called the hotel stop "basically a hygiene break. In the middle of his heroic national marathon, Bob Dole took a break to clean up with a shower and a shave," he said. "As filthy as Bill Clinton's campaign has been, he might as well consider cleaning up too."
Dole and his wife Elizabeth then went to the First United Methodist Church in the Mission Valley section of San Diego.

Although he got a late start on Sunday, Dole set out to resume his hectic pace with campaign appearances in the state through to midnight. He was to be joined at some points by his running mate, Jack Kemp.
He heads off after midnight to Arizona, then on to New Mexico, Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Iowa.
Dole intends to finish his campaign on Tuesday in Independence, Missouri, the hometown of Harry Truman, who came from behind to win the 1948 presidential race.
He will then cast his vote in his hometown of Russell, Kansas.
Dole is hoping his grueling campaign push will help him narrow a persistent poll deficit against President Clinton and carry him on to victory.
"We are going to work around the clock, around the clock, around the clock," Dole told the volunteers in San Diego.

California is the largest prize of the contest and has been steadily pursued by Dole. But Dole continues to trail Clinton, who has made the state one of his top political priorities throughout his presidency.

An internal campaign poll finished on Saturday showed Dole trailed Clinton by 4 percentage points in the state, Dole California adviser Ken Khachigian said. The poll of likely voters among a group of 400 voters surveyed had a five-point margin of error.
It remained to be seen whether Dole could close the gap, but state Republicans were likely to at least hold their own in congressional races, he said.
In working the phone banks, Dole spoke with a voter named Randy. "Well I just wanted to say hello and have a good day and a good year, and next year you'll get a tax cut," Dole said.
Upon learning Randy, his wife and daughter had already cast their votes for Dole, the candidate joked, "It's three already. We're ahead."
Nationally, both Clinton and Dole picked up support on Saturday, leaving Clinton's lead unchanged at 3.8 percentage points in the Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll released on Sunday.
Clinton scored 43.5 percent, Dole polled 39.7 percent, Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was the choice of 7.2 percent and 7.7 percent remained undecided.
Other polls showed Clinton with a wider lead with two days to go until Election Day. But several also showed the race narrowing.
